content: The data for some countries originates from small, localized, or regional studies. These data are heterogeneous in terms of methodology, formats, and other factors. However, we developed specific approaches to address this heterogeneity, as detailed in the annexes. Additionally, all quantitative 24-hour dietary recall data are inherently imprecise and may be subject to bias. For our global food item list, we excluded items and subgroups that were rarely consumed in most or all countries for which we had data. However, some of these excluded items, such as non-liver organ meats, seafood, snails, and insects, may hold significant national or local importance. Similarly, there are various wild and foraged fruits and vegetables that are nutrient-dense. Where such items are available and culturally acceptable, they should be included in analyses that support the development of national or local food-based dietary recommendations. For practical reasons, we selected U.S. food composition databases as our primary sources, even though the nutrient composition of many foods varies geographically. For breast milk nutrient composition, we used values from the USDA Food Pattern Modeling Report (2020 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee and Food Pattern Modeling Team, 2020). However, this source did not include values for DHA and EPA. The primary sources we used reported zero values for DHA and EPA, which we questioned. Although we initially planned to report results for DHA and EPA, we ultimately chose not to, as these were not target nutrients. Data on linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid were unavailable for many foods. In such cases, we used data on undifferentiated 18:2 and 18:3 fatty acids, which may have slightly biased the nutrient profiles for these two nutrients (potentially overestimating them). However, we judged that this was unlikely to have substantially impacted the results. Matching fish to food composition data posed particular challenges because fish are often poorly described in dietary datasets. Additionally, some common fish names can refer to a wide variety of species. When developing nutrient profiles, it is ideal to weight individual food items based on their relative contribution to total consumption within a food subgroup, considering both frequency and quantity consumed. However, due to the lack of globally representative dietary data for infants and young children (IYC), we instead weighted items based on the proportion of countries in which each item was reported to be consumed by IYC. This ensured that items commonly consumed across many geographies were more heavily weighted, while those reported in fewer countries were less heavily weighted. However, we cannot determine how our weighting compares to the ideal. Although we reviewed nutrient distributions within food subgroups and excluded some outlier items (both true outliers and suspect values), several subgroups, particularly those with a small number of items, exhibited heterogeneity in certain nutrients, making the subgroup profiles less meaningful. For example: In some grain subgroups, the inclusion of nixtamalized maize products slightly increased calcium values. However, the number of items in these subgroups was not extremely small, and the nutrient profiles were not strongly affected. Among the few high-fat fruits, avocado is high in folate, and coconut is high in iron, which influenced the nutrient profile. Fresh coconut may also be consumed in smaller quantities than avocado, yet we created a median serving size for both foods based on higher observed medians, which may have been more appropriate for avocado. For soy foods, we used the same representative item for tofu as the USDA did in their food pattern modeling exercise for IYC. This tofu type is coagulated with calcium and magnesium salts, which affected the subgroup nutrient profile. For fish (both small and large fish subgroups), there is very high true variability for some nutrients. Additionally, for the food subgroup of small fish eaten with bones, we included several species available in global markets, as well as some specific to Eastern and Southern Africa, resulting in uneven geographic representation within the subgroup. For several problem nutrients, especially calcium, iron, and zinc, there are dietary and non-dietary factors that influence absorption. It was not feasible for us to take a nuanced approach that accounted for enhancers and inhibitors of absorption and other factors. We accepted the assumptions about nutrient absorption inherent to the selected nutrient reference values (NRVs), based on the principle that our models allowed ample amounts of all food subgroups, enabling food patterns in solutions to resemble mixed diets as described in the reference value documents. For infants aged 9 months, this led to food patterns with minimal flesh foods, as the Optifood software minimizes protein as a proxy for cost once all nutrient targets are met. We addressed this by performing sensitivity analyses assuming a lower absorption level for iron. By using subgroup nutrient profiles, we modeled food subgroups at the mean. That is, the profiles were developed as weighted averages of sets of food items, and our modeling did not explore the nutrient variability within each subgroup or how choices within food subgroups would affect nutrient gaps. The Optifood software includes a module to address this issue of variability, but it was not feasible for us to explore this. As a result, our findings should be interpreted cautiously, recognizing that they provide a general picture but have inherent false precision. Although we modeled a large number of scenarios, time and cost constraints prevented us from modeling all desirable scenarios. Key limitations included: Assuming the same proportion of energy from breast milk for all IYC in a given age group, rather than modeling multiple proportions. Not modeling mixed feeding with breast milk and formula. Modeling best-case food patterns at three energy levels for each age/feeding group but restricting modifications to one energy level per age group, based on the estimated energy requirement (EER) for an average-sized child at the midpoint of the age range. Not modeling several plausible scenarios, such as eliminating additional combinations of food subgroups (e.g., both whole grains and flesh foods simultaneously), eliminating rarely consumed food subgroups (e.g., berries, high-fat fruits, soy foods, liver, and small fish with bones), increasing staple foods while restricting to one type of staple food, including multiple types of sentinel unhealthy foods simultaneously, or including sentinel unhealthy foods while eliminating various nutrient-dense food groups. Any of these combination scenarios could result in more numerous or deeper gaps in target and non-target nutrients. Scenarios approximating real-world patterns embodied some of these combinations. Our analyses allowed us to address several key questions: 1. Can target nutrient needs be met with unfortified best-case food patterns? Except for the smallest infants in the youngest age group, unfortified foods consumed in feasible amounts can meet all target nutrient needs except for iron in infancy. However, this requires access to diverse foods from all food groups and the consumption of diverse vegetable and protein food subgroups. 2. What happens when food groups or subgroups are eliminated? For 9-month-old infants, eliminating whole grains, vegetables, or various protein food subgroups resulted in numerous nutrient gaps. For older IYC, eliminating all fruits and vegetables, all flesh foods, or all animal-source foods more broadly was most problematic. 3. What happens when staple foods are monotonous or increased in quantity? Restricting the type or increasing the amount of staple foods caused multiple nutrient gaps for the youngest age group. However, it did not introduce additional nutrient gaps for older IYC when food patterns included the diverse nutrient-dense foods available in the best-case scenarios. 4. What happens if unhealthy foods or beverages are added? For 9-month-old infants, there was little room for unhealthy foods or beverages. However, for older IYC, there was space in the diet for a daily serving of unhealthy foods when food patterns also included diverse nutrient-dense foods. 5. What are the nutrient gaps when approximating real-world food patterns? There were gaps for B vitamins, choline, and minerals in all three settings, with more numerous and larger gaps in Bangladesh and Malawi. These gaps were larger than those in model solutions. 6. Can fortified items fill all nutrient gaps? Fortified items had diverse impacts depending on their composition and energy content per dose, resulting in varying patterns of displacement. For the youngest infants, SQ-LNS and Super Cereal Plus displaced most foods other than breast milk, resulting in nutrient gaps. For modeled food patterns, all products reduced gaps for vitamin D. Super Cereal Plus did not provide other benefits. MNPs and SQ-LNS reduced or eliminated gaps for iron. For real-world food patterns, all three fortified items reduced or eliminated gaps for B vitamins and iron, with the best results for iron achieved with MNPs, followed by SQ-LNS. MNPs and SQ-LNS eliminated gaps for zinc and copper, and SQ-LNS reduced or eliminated the gap for calcium. However, there were remaining nutrient gaps in each setting. In conclusion, except for iron and the smallest infants, it is possible to meet all target nutrient needs from unfortified foods consumed in feasible quantities. However, the best-case food patterns achieving this are very different from those found in many real-world settings. For the youngest infants, the best-case food patterns include very small amounts of starchy staple foods. For all IYC, the best-case patterns are rich in diverse vegetables, include flesh foods, and exclude refined grains. Several examples approximating real-world food patterns had a lower percentage of energy from vegetables and protein foods, resulting in numerous nutrient gaps. Fortified items provided only a partial solution.
